Where it began

Jonty Rhodes was born in Pietermaritzburg on 27 July 1969. He went to Maritzburg College and then the University of Natal, playing his club cricket for the university side. Cricket was not his only game. He was good enough at hockey to play for South Africa, and was named in the squad for the 1992 Olympics in Barcelona, though the team did not qualify to make the trip.

The player

He arrived on the international stage at the 1992 World Cup, running out Craig McDermott in his first one-day match, in Sydney. Less than two weeks later, in Brisbane, came the moment that made his name. Inzamam-ul-Haq was sent back on a single, and Rhodes raced in from backward point with the ball, beat him to the stumps and dived headlong to break them. Jim Fenwick's photograph of that dive went round the world.

His Test career began at Kingsmead in Durban in November 1992, with 41 and 26 not out against India. His first Test hundred, an unbeaten 101 at Moratuwa in the 1993–1994 season, saved a match against Sri Lanka. In 52 Tests up to August 2000 he made 2,532 runs at 35.66, with three hundreds, 17 fifties and a best of 117, and held 34 catches. He was part of the side that won the 1998 ICC KnockOut Trophy, South Africa's first ICC title. An injury cut short his last World Cup, in 2003.

What made him special

The fielding, first and last. Backward point was his patch, and his catching, his stopping and his throwing all set him apart. In a one-day game against West Indies in Mumbai in 1993 he held five catches, then a world record for a fielder. He was also the first South African to reach 100 one-day catches. With the bat he was quick between the wickets and fond of the reverse sweep, and is credited with the first reverse sweep to go for six.

He did turn his arm over in Tests, without ever troubling the scorers' wicket column. Perhaps that was only fair. He had already done enough to the batsmen.

Away from the middle

After his playing days he turned to coaching, fielding above all, with South Africa, Mumbai Indians, Kings XI Punjab and, from 2023, Lucknow Super Giants. He helped Kenya prepare for the 2011 World Cup and in 2024 became mentor to Pokhara Avengers in the new Nepal Premier League. He also worked as a commentator, and in 2013 South African Tourism made him its ambassador in India.

Wisden named him a Cricketer of the Year in 1999. In 2004 television viewers voted him 29th in a list of the Great South Africans, and in 2021 Invertis University gave him an honorary doctorate.

And finally

Plenty of cricketers are remembered for a hundred or a five-wicket haul. Rhodes is remembered for a run-out, and for spending a good part of his career a few feet off the ground.
